Optical character recognition has a long history, and the problems it faces on a screen are
not the problems it faces on a page. A scanned document arrives with paper texture,
skew, and bleed-through from the reverse side.

A screen region arrives clean, perfectly axis aligned, and free of noise, but it arrives at
whatever size the display happened to render it. That difference matters more than it first
appears.

Recognition engines trained on scanned pages expect glyphs roughly the size they would
be at three hundred dots per inch. Text rendered for a screen at ordinary reading size is
far smaller than that, so the most useful thing a preprocessing stage can do is make the
image bigger before the engine sees it.

Upscaling alone will not invent detail that the renderer never drew. What it does instead
is give the recognition model the spatial context its convolutions were designed around.
